items.prompt: What is the main function of the somatosensory system?

options.label: Perceiving external stimuli, internal stimuli, and regulating body position and balance
options.feedback: Correct. The somatosensory system handles these three main jobs, including touch and knowing where your body is.

options.label: Only detecting pain and temperature
options.feedback: Pain and temperature are part of it, but the system also handles touch and balance. This option leaves out most of its work.

options.label: Only sending signals from the skin to the brain
options.feedback: It does send signals, but it also perceives internal stimuli and regulates body position and balance, so this is too narrow.

options.label: Controlling voluntary muscle movements
options.feedback: That is the motor system's job. The somatosensory system senses, it does not command muscles to move.

items.ok_line: The somatosensory system senses outside, inside, and body position.
items.ko_line: It does far more than just pain or skin signals.
items.exp_text: The somatosensory system perceives external stimuli like touch, internal stimuli, and regulates body position and balance through proprioception. It is a broad sensory system, not limited to one type of feeling.

items.prompt: Which of these is a general somatic sense, unlike sight or hearing?

options.label: Sight
options.feedback: Sight is a special sense, not a general somatic one. The general somatic sense here is touch.

options.label: Hearing
options.feedback: Hearing is also a special sense. Touch is the general somatic sense.

options.label: Touch
options.feedback: Correct. Touch is a general somatic sense, while sight, smell, taste, hearing, and balance are special senses.

options.label: Balance
options.feedback: Balance is listed among the special senses, not as a general somatic sense.

items.ok_line: Touch is a general somatic sense; the others are special.
items.ko_line: Sight, hearing, and balance are special, not general.
items.exp_text: Touch belongs to the general somatic senses, alongside the sense of the body's position, while sight, smell, taste, hearing, and balance are the special senses. The somatosensory system handles the general ones.

items.prompt: Where are the cutaneous receptors for touch located?

options.label: In the muscles
options.feedback: Muscles have proprioceptors, not the cutaneous receptors used for touch. Those are in the skin.

options.label: In the skin
options.feedback: Correct. Cutaneous receptors are special sensory receptors found in the skin that detect pressure, vibration, pain, and temperature.

options.label: In the joints
options.feedback: Joints have proprioceptors for position sense, but touch receptors are in the skin.

options.label: In the spinal cord
options.feedback: The spinal cord carries signals, but the touch receptors themselves sit in the skin.

items.ok_line: Cutaneous receptors live in the skin.
items.ko_line: Muscles and joints sense position, not touch.
items.exp_text: The sense of touch uses special sensory receptors in the skin, called cutaneous receptors. They include mechanoreceptors for pressure and vibration, nociceptors for pain, and thermoreceptors for temperature.

options.label: Light touch and vibration
options.feedback: Light touch and vibration are mechanosensory information, not pain. Nociceptors are specialized for pain signals.

options.label: Normal temperature in the skin
options.feedback: Normal temperature is relayed by thermoreceptors. Nociceptors handle pain, not everyday temperature.

options.label: Sustained skin stretch
options.feedback: Sustained skin stretch is detected by bulbous corpuscles, a type of mechanoreceptor, not nociceptors.

options.label: Pain signals
options.feedback: Correct. Nociceptors are specialized receptors for signals of pain, including pain from harmful stimuli.

items.ko_line: Touch, temperature, and stretch have their own receptors.
items.exp_text: Nociceptors are specialized receptors that detect pain, including pain from harmful stimuli. They are one of the two subdivisions of the somatosensory system, along with mechanosensory touch.

items.prompt: Which receptor is found in the dermal papillae and reacts to light touch?

options.label: Tactile corpuscles
options.feedback: Correct. Tactile corpuscles sit in the dermal papillae and respond to light touch and moderate vibration.

options.label: Merkel cell nerve endings
options.feedback: Merkel cells react to deep static touch and low vibrations, and they are found in the basal epidermis, not the dermal papillae.

options.label: Pacinian corpuscles
options.feedback: Pacinian corpuscles react to sudden stimuli and high-frequency vibration, and they are not located in the dermal papillae.

options.label: Bulbous corpuscles
options.feedback: Bulbous corpuscles respond to sustained skin stretch, not light touch, and are not in the dermal papillae.

items.ok_line: Tactile corpuscles handle light touch in the papillae.
items.ko_line: Each corpuscle has its own location and trigger.
items.exp_text: Tactile corpuscles are located in the dermal papillae of the skin. They react to moderate vibration (10–50 Hz) and light touch, and are especially common in fingertips and lips.

items.prompt: Which receptor is responsible for the ability to read Braille?

options.label: Merkel cell nerve endings
options.feedback: Merkel cells detect deep static touch and shapes, but they are not the ones credited with Braille reading. That is the tactile corpuscle.

options.label: Tactile corpuscles
options.feedback: Correct. Tactile corpuscles react to gentle stimuli and are responsible for the ability to read Braille.

options.label: Pacinian corpuscles
options.feedback: Pacinian corpuscles detect gross touch and vibrations, not the fine gentle stimuli needed for Braille.

options.label: Bulbous corpuscles
options.feedback: Bulbous corpuscles sense skin stretch and object slippage, not the light touch used in Braille.

items.ok_line: Tactile corpuscles make Braille reading possible.
items.ko_line: Other receptors handle deeper touch or vibration.
items.exp_text: Tactile corpuscles respond in quick action potentials to gentle stimuli, which is why they are found in fingertips and lips and are responsible for reading Braille.

items.prompt: Which receptor reacts only to sudden stimuli and quickly ignores constant pressure like clothes?

options.label: Merkel cell nerve endings
options.feedback: Merkel cells respond to pressures over long periods, so they do not ignore constant pressure. That is the Pacinian corpuscle.

options.label: Tactile corpuscles
options.feedback: Tactile corpuscles react to light touch and vibration, not specifically to sudden stimuli or ignoring constant pressure.

options.label: Pacinian corpuscles
options.feedback: Correct. Pacinian corpuscles react only to sudden stimuli, so steady pressure from clothes is quickly ignored.

options.label: Bulbous corpuscles
options.feedback: Bulbous corpuscles respond slowly to sustained stretch, so they do not ignore constant pressure.

items.ko_line: Merkel and bulbous cells handle constant input.
items.exp_text: Pacinian corpuscles are most sensitive to vibrations around 250 Hz and react only to sudden stimuli. Because of this, constant pressure like clothing is quickly ignored after the initial touch.

items.prompt: Which receptor responds to sustained skin stretch and helps with the feeling of object slippage?

options.label: Tactile corpuscles
options.feedback: Tactile corpuscles respond to light touch and vibration, not sustained stretch or slippage.

options.label: Pacinian corpuscles
options.feedback: Pacinian corpuscles react to sudden stimuli and vibration, not slow sustained stretch.

options.label: Merkel cell nerve endings
options.feedback: Merkel cells detect deep static touch and low vibrations, not sustained stretch or slippage.

options.label: Bulbous corpuscles
options.feedback: Correct. Bulbous corpuscles respond slowly to sustained skin stretch and are responsible for the feeling of object slippage.

items.ko_line: Tactile and Pacinian cells react quickly, not slowly.
items.exp_text: Bulbous corpuscles respond slowly and to sustained skin stretch. This makes them key for sensing when an object is slipping and for controlling finger position and movement.

items.prompt: Where does the primary somatosensory cortex lie?

options.label: In the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
options.feedback: Correct. The postcentral gyrus sits in the parietal lobe, and its cortex is the primary somatosensory cortex called S1.

options.label: In the temporal lobe near the ears
options.feedback: The temporal lobe handles hearing, not touch. The somatosensory cortex is in the parietal lobe.

options.label: In the occipital lobe at the back
options.feedback: The occipital lobe is for vision, not touch. Somatosensory cortex is parietal.

options.label: In the frontal lobe behind the forehead
options.feedback: The frontal lobe is involved in movement and planning, not the primary touch cortex.

items.ok_line: Primary somatosensory cortex is in the parietal lobe.
items.ko_line: Touch is processed in the parietal, not temporal, occipital, or frontal.
items.exp_text: The primary somatosensory cortex, called S1, is in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe. It receives touch, pain, and temperature information from the body.

items.prompt: Which part of the brain processes texture information?

options.label: Area S2
options.feedback: Area S2 processes light touch, pain, and visceral sensation, but texture is processed in BA1.

options.label: BA1
options.feedback: Correct. BA1 processes texture information, while BA2 handles size and shape.

options.label: BA2
options.feedback: BA2 processes size and shape, not texture. BA1 is for texture.

options.label: The insular cortex
options.feedback: The insula is involved in bodily self-awareness and conveying sensual touch, but texture is processed in BA1.

items.ko_line: BA2 does shape, BA1 does texture.
items.exp_text: Within the somatosensory cortex, BA1 processes texture information, while BA2 handles size and shape. BA3b distributes the info to these areas.
